subject: Private endpoints: outbound fingerprinting, SNI inspection, and allowlist requirements

Raj — thanks for the clear list. I attached a CSV template with the fields your firewall team usually asks for and a short narrative below. Attaching: redwood_private_allowlist_template.csv

High-level answers:
- Outbound IPs: For private deployments we publish two groups: (A) Control-plane egress (limited set of static IPs for telemetry, metrics, and control API calls) and (B) Data egress (model inference outbound calls to model shard services and optional upstreams). Most customers allow the control-plane IPs as static CIDRs and map data egress to either a small pool of customer-owned NAT IPs or a short-lived Redwood-egress pool.
- TLS & SNI inspection: Redwood’s private runtime accepts TLS from customer workloads. We recommend NOT performing TLS interception for connections to customer-managed control-plane endpoints because that breaks mTLS and certificate pinning. For egress to public model registries or external tool integrations, interception is tolerated but may break mTLS flows. If your proxy inspects SNI, please preserve the original SNI header — our TLS termination relies on SNI in some multi-tenant routing cases.
- Ephemeral rotation / maintenance: We publish planned rotations 7 days in advance in the customer portal for Dedicated/Private customers. For emergency rotations we provide a short outage window and temporary allowlist alternatives (pre-authorized CIDR that we can use during the handover).

Next steps:
1) Please have your firewall team fill the attached CSV.
2) Marcus, can you add the control-plane CIDRs + known service FQDNs to the CSV and confirm ports?
3) Raj, once we have that we’ll provide the SOC2 evidence checklist and an example ip-rotation schedule.

Best,
Vanessa Ortiz

Raj / Vanessa — adding a few technical clarifications for the firewall and network ops folks.

TL;DR: Control-plane is static-ish; data-plane may use customer NAT or a small Redwood ephemeral pool depending on deployment mode. Ports and TLS notes below.

1) Control-plane (recommended allowlist)
- IPs: 52.24.198.0/28, 34.82.16.0/28 (example; see attached CSV for canonical list)
- Ports: 443 (HTTPS), 8530 (optional health & metrics over TLS), 5222 (agent heartbeat over mTLS if you enable agent connectivity)
- TLS: mTLS on control-plane registration; no TLS interception.

2) Data-plane egress patterns (choose one):
- Mode A (Customer NAT): Redwood nodes will use your NAT IPs for all outbound. You then only need to allow destinations (FQDNs) instead of Redwood IPs. Recommend: allow TLS egress to *.redwood-inference.net:443 and specific external integrations.
- Mode B (Redwood egresster pool): small set of ephemeral IPs rotated weekly. We provide an API to fetch the currently active egress IPs and also publish rotation windows. If you select this, allow CIDRs in the CSV and consider short TTL DNS rules on your proxy to avoid stale mappings.

3) SNI and TLS interception guidance
- If your proxy performs TLS interception: allowlist exceptions for control-plane endpoints. Interception is OK for outbound requests to third-party services but NOT for the control-plane registration endpoint.
- For SNI-preserving inspection: ensure the proxy forwards SNI unchanged. If your proxy rewrites or suppresses SNI, some multi-host certificate routing may fail.

4) Deep packet inspection & DLP
- If DLP tools require plaintext access, we recommend performing it at an upstream egress point that is aware of mTLS exceptions. Otherwise, do it on non-control-plane traffic only.

Attachments referenced: redwood_private_allowlist_template.csv (canonical CIDRs & FQDNs).

Marcus Lin
Senior Infrastructure Security Engineer, Redwood Inference
